question: What mnemonic helps identify the failed engine after an asymmetric power loss?
explanation: AFM 3.7.1: once directional control is re-established, the pilot feels no rudder-pedal force on the side of the failed engine — "dead foot, dead engine".

question: With one engine inoperative, in which direction does the airplane yaw and roll (with coordinated controls)?

options.text: In the direction of the rudder trim setting only
Away from the failed engine, toward the operating engine
Only in yaw, never in roll

explanation: AFM 3.7.1: one engine inoperative means an asymmetric loss of thrust, resulting in uncommanded yaw and roll toward the dead engine.

question: Which engine is considered the "critical" engine on the DA 42 NG, with respect to handling and performance?

options.text: Neither — both engines are equally critical
Whichever engine has the higher total time

explanation: AFM 3.7.2 and 4A.6.21 both state that the left-hand engine is considered the critical engine for handling and performance purposes.

question: At what minimum propeller speed can the propeller still be feathered?
explanation: AFM 7.9.2: feathering is only possible at propeller speeds above 1300 RPM; below that, propeller pitch remains below the start-lock position.

question: What is the first step of the engine securing (feathering) procedure after identifying and verifying the affected engine?

options.text: Set ENGINE MASTER of the affected engine to OFF
Set the FUEL SELECTOR of the affected engine to OFF
Set the ALTERNATOR of the affected engine to OFF

explanation: AFM 3.7.3: ENGINE MASTER OFF shuts down and feathers the engine; the fuel selector must never be used to shut down an engine, to avoid damaging the high-pressure fuel pump.

question: Why must an engine never be shut down using the FUEL SELECTOR valve?

options.text: It triggers an unwanted fire warning
It can damage the high-pressure fuel pump
It prevents the propeller from feathering
It disables the ECU backup battery

explanation: AFM 3.7.3 and 4A.6.14 both caution that shutting down with the fuel selector, rather than ENGINE MASTER, can damage the high-pressure fuel pump.

question: After feathering, why can the remaining fuel in the secured engine's tank still be useful?

options.text: It is used only to keep the fuel probes calibrated
It cannot be used and must be left in the tank until landing
It can be used by the remaining engine via CROSSFEED, to extend range and maintain lateral balance
It automatically dumps overboard to reduce weight

explanation: A note under AFM 3.7.3 explains that the remaining fuel in the secured engine's tank can be drawn by the operating engine via CROSSFEED.

question: If a POWER lever is set to a low setting after securing an engine and the landing gear warning horn sounds, what mutes it?

options.text: Switching the ALTERNATOR of the secured engine back ON
Setting the POWER lever of the secured engine forward as required

explanation: AFM 3.7.3 notes that advancing the secured engine's POWER lever forward mutes the retracted-gear warning horn triggered by a low power-lever position.

question: What is the maximum restart airspeed using the starter, for an in-flight restart?

options.text: 100 KIAS, or the airspeed for a stationary propeller, whichever is lower

explanation: AFM 3.7.4: the starter must only be engaged with a stationary propeller, at or below 100 KIAS.

question: For a windmilling restart, what is the minimum airspeed required?
explanation: AFM 3.7.4: a windmilling restart requires airspeed between 125 and 145 KIAS — below 125 KIAS the propeller may not windmill continuously.

question: For a windmilling restart, what is the maximum airspeed permitted?
explanation: AFM 3.7.4: above 145 KIAS a windmilling restart can overspeed the propeller; the window is 125-145 KIAS.

question: During an in-flight restart with the starter, why must the starter never be engaged while the propeller is windmilling?

options.text: It has no effect either way, so the caution is precautionary only
It will always overspeed the propeller past 2500 RPM
Engaging the starter on a windmilling propeller is prohibited by a specific caution in the AFM

explanation: AFM 3.7.4 gives a direct caution: do not engage the starter when the propeller is windmilling; below 100 KIAS the propeller may windmill intermittently, so care is needed to confirm it is stationary.

question: If an engine fails during the ground roll on take-off, what is the first response?

options.text: Abort the take-off — POWER levers both IDLE, maintain directional control with rudder, brake as required
Continue the take-off using MAX power on the operating engine
Feather the affected engine before reducing power
Retract the flaps immediately to reduce drag

explanation: AFM 3.7.5(a): an engine failure during the ground roll calls for an aborted take-off — both power levers IDLE, directional control by rudder, and brakes as required.

question: If an engine fails after lift-off and a continued take-off is attempted, what airspeed should be flown?
explanation: AFM 3.7.5(b): a continued take-off with an engine failure targets vYSE = 85 KIAS as the airspeed for best single-engine climb.

question: A continued take-off after an engine failure is not recommended if the steady rate of climb is less than what percentage gradient?
explanation: AFM 3.7.5(b) warns against continuing the take-off if the one-engine-inoperative climb gradient (per 5.3.8) is less than 3.3%.

question: During an engine failure in initial climb, what side-slip / bank condition should be established once directional control is regained?

options.text: Full ball deflection toward the failed engine, wings level
Zero bank, full rudder deflection maintained
A full ball toward the good engine with 15° of bank
Minimum / zero sideslip: approximately half a ball toward the good engine, 3° to 5° bank

explanation: AFM 3.7.6(a) directs establishing minimum/zero sideslip: about half a ball toward the operative engine with 3-5° of bank.

question: During an engine failure in flight (not initial climb), to what load should the operative engine be increased?
explanation: AFM 3.7.6(b) directs increasing the operative engine to up to 92% load — the maximum continuous power rating — while securing the failed engine.

question: During an approach with one engine inoperative, what is the final approach speed with flaps UP, up to 1900 kg?
explanation: AFM 3.7.7 gives one-engine-inoperative final approach speeds of 86 KIAS (flaps UP), 84 KIAS (flaps APP) and 84 KIAS (flaps LDG), all up to 1900 kg.

question: For a one-engine-inoperative landing, why are flap settings greater than UP not recommended unless a safe landing is assured?

options.text: They disable the variable elevator stop
Higher flap settings increase the loss of altitude during a transition to a one-engine-inoperative go-around
They increase the stall speed beyond vMCA

explanation: AFM 3.7.7 warns that one-engine-inoperative approaches with more than flaps UP are not recommended unless "making the field" is assured, because of the altitude loss during a subsequent go-around.

question: Below what altitude AGL is a one-engine-inoperative go-around / balked landing NOT recommended to be initiated?
explanation: AFM 3.7.8 recommends against initiating a one-engine-inoperative go-around below a minimum of 800 ft AGL.

question: During a one-engine-inoperative go-around, what airspeed is targeted?
explanation: AFM 3.7.8: the go-around with one engine inoperative uses MAX power on the operative engine and vYSE = 85 KIAS.

question: If a positive rate of climb cannot be established during a one-engine-inoperative go-around, and landing off-airfield above 1900 kg is required, what is the minimum approach speed with flaps APP?
explanation: AFM 3.7.8: above 1900 kg the minimum off-field approach speed is 88 KIAS with flaps APP (86 KIAS with flaps LDG); up to 1900 kg it is 84 KIAS with either flap setting.

question: During sustained flight with one engine inoperative, what is the minimum airspeed to maintain directional control with flaps UP?
explanation: AFM 3.7.9: with flaps UP the minimum controllable airspeed is vMCA = 71 KIAS; with flaps APP it is 68 KIAS.

question: During sustained one-engine-inoperative flight, what can prolonged excessive sideslip or bank angle cause?

options.text: Loss of the standby attitude module
Automatic engine shutdown by the ECU
Fuel starvation, normally advised by a LOW FUEL indication

explanation: AFM 3.7.9 cautions that prolonged excessive sideslip/bank can cause fuel starvation; the response is to return to coordinated flight or use CROSSFEED on the affected engine.

question: During a full engines-out (both engines) landing, what is the minimum approach speed with flaps APP, up to 1900 kg?
explanation: AFM 3.8: up to 1900 kg the engines-out minimum approach speed is 84 KIAS with either flaps APP or flaps LDG; above 1900 kg it rises to 88 KIAS (APP) or 86 KIAS (LDG).

question: For an engines-out landing above 1900 kg with flaps LDG selected, what is the minimum approach speed?
explanation: AFM 3.8: above 1900 kg the minimum approach speed is 88 KIAS with flaps APP but only 86 KIAS with flaps LDG.

question: Under the demonstration of engine shutdown/restart in training, what is the maximum altitude permitted?
explanation: AFM 4A.6.21 sets the training demonstration altitude band between 3,000 ft AGL minimum and 10,000 ft pressure altitude maximum.

question: Under the demonstration of engine shutdown/restart in training, what is the minimum altitude permitted?
explanation: AFM 4A.6.21: the minimum altitude for the training demonstration is 3,000 ft AGL, with a maximum of 10,000 ft pressure altitude.

question: During the training demonstration, at what airspeed is the airplane trimmed before the selected engine is shut down?
explanation: AFM 4A.6.21: the airplane is trimmed to 100 KIAS in level flight before the ENGINE MASTER of the selected engine is switched OFF.

question: During the training demonstration, once the engine is shut down and idled, between what airspeeds is it stabilized before restart?
explanation: AFM 4A.6.21: after shutdown, airspeed is stabilized between 90 and 100 KIAS before the ENGINE MASTER is switched back ON to unfeather and restart.

question: Under the AFM 5.3.8 one-engine-inoperative climb performance conditions, what load is set on the remaining engine?
explanation: AFM 5.3.8 states the OEI climb performance tables assume 92% load on the remaining engine, dead engine feathered and secured, flaps UP, gear retracted, at vYSE = 85 KIAS.

question: Under the AFM 5.3.8 one-engine-inoperative climb performance conditions, what sideslip condition is assumed?

options.text: Two balls out toward the dead engine
Half ball toward the dead engine

explanation: AFM 5.3.8 assumes a sideslip of one ball out, with a maximum of 5° bank, matching the technique taught in 3.7.6.

question: At maximum take-off mass (1900 kg), sea level, ISA conditions, roughly what one-engine-inoperative rate of climb does the AFM 5.3.8 table show?
explanation: AFM 5.3.8's OEI climb table shows approximately 269 ft/min at 1900 kg, sea level, ISA — much less than the roughly 1337 ft/min available with both engines operating in the same conditions.

question: Compared to the all-engines-operating rate of climb at MTOM/SL/ISA (about 1337 ft/min with flaps UP), what does losing one engine do to climb performance?

options.text: It reverses the climb into a descent at any weight
It reduces the climb rate by roughly 80%, to only about 269 ft/min
It has almost no effect, since the DA 42 NG is certified for OEI climb equal to AEO climb
It roughly halves the climb rate, to about 670 ft/min

explanation: Comparing AFM 5.3.7 (about 1337 ft/min, all engines, flaps UP, MTOM/SL/ISA) with AFM 5.3.8 (about 269 ft/min, one engine inoperative, same conditions) shows how severely climb performance is degraded by an engine failure.

question: Why does the AFM caution that a continued take-off after an engine failure has to be avoided if at all possible?

options.text: Because the ECU automatically shuts down the remaining engine after 90 seconds of asymmetric power
Because it is legally prohibited under JAR-23 in the Normal Category
Because ambient conditions like turbulence, crosswind and wind shear, plus pilot skill, may make the resulting climb performance insufficient even when the calculated gradient looks adequate
Because a continued take-off always requires more runway than is available at any airport

explanation: AFM 3.7.5(b) explains that even when the 3.3% gradient criterion is met, real-world factors can make the climb performance insufficient, so a continued take-off should be avoided whenever possible.
